Vs.
The Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development, Govt. of J Bangladesh and others---------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, :—This rule is directed against the impugned action of the respondents in taking over an urban premises as an abandoned property under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972. Facts relevant for the disposal of the rule in brief, are that the petitioner entered into an agreement for the purchase of premises in question with one Anwarul Haque on 18.12.70 and pursuant to the said agreement paid a sum of Taka 50,000/- to the vendor as earnest money which was duly acknowledged in the agreement itself and pursuant to the said agreement the vendor delivered possession of the properly to the petitioner and since then he has been in possession of the said properly. It was further agreed between the vendor and the petitioner that after obtaining the necessary income tax clearance and other papers, the sale deed would be executed and registered on receipt of the balance of consideration money of Taka 25,000/- and in the event of failure or refusal to execute and register the sale deed the petitioner Would be entitled to get it registered through court. The vendor having failed to perform his part of the obligation, the petitioner was obliged to institute a suit for specific performance of contract in the first court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca on 1.4.74 being title suit No. 126 of 1974, wherein the vendor was made defendant No. 1 and the Government of Bangladesh was made defendant No. 2. The Government of Bangladesh appeared in the said suit through the Government Pleader and obtained several adjournments to file the written statement but ultimately did not file any. Thereafter the suit was decreed exparte in favour of the petitioner on 4.9.74 by the first Court of sub-ordinate judge, Dacca and defendant No. 1 (the vendor ) was directed to execute and register the same on receipt of the balance consideration money within 30 days in default of which the petitioner would get the sale-deed executed and registered through Court by depositing the balance consideration money in Court Certified copy of judgment and decree passed in the said suit has been annexed to the petition as Annexures `E' and `E-1'. The vendor, the defendant No. 1 having failed to comply with the direction of the Court, the Subordinate Judge executed and registered the sale deed on be-half of the vendor in the Sadar Sub-Registry, Dacca on 14.1.1975, certified copy of which has been annexed to the petition as Annexure It was further stated by the petitioner that while he was thus in peaceful possession of the premises in question, Mr. Aftabuddin, the then Deputy Secretary of the Government of Bangladesh forcibly evicted the petitioner from the premises on 15.1.75. It was further asserted by the petitioner that the petitioner produced before Mr. Aftalyuddin the certified copy of the sale-deed and the decree of the Court to establish his lawful ownership and possession in the property. That subsequently, the petitioner moved the authorities concerned by filing representations and also in person but failed to get any redress of his legitimate grievances. Being aggrieved, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 3. Mr Moinul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has submitted that the properly in question by virtue of the court's decree rightfully belonged to the petitioner who was also in lawful possession of the same and the property was never declared as, an abandoned property and the petitioner eras illegally evicted from the premises in violation of the law. Mr. M. M. Haque, the learned Assistant Attorney General in reply submitted that the property having vested in the Government as an abandoned property, the court decree had no validity in the eye of law and the petitioner having no legal right to be in possession of the said property was rightly evicted by the respondents. 

 5. In support of his arguments Mr. Moinul Hossain has drawn our attention to the supplementary-affidavit filed by the petitioner and the annexures 'V' and 'Z' to the said affidavit. It appears from the said annexures that the petitioner was served with a notice by the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (south), Dacca as early as 8.7.72 asking him to show cause why he should not be directed to surrender the property since it was an abandoned property. The petitioner duly showed cause on 15.7.72 wherein he asserted that he was in lawful possession of the property by virtue of a deed of agreement ( Annexure 'Y' ). Thereafter the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (south) Dacca by his order dated 26.2.73 after considering the reply of the petitioner ordered that the premises in question be dropped from the abandoned list in favour of the petitioner '(Annexure 'Z'). This fact has not been denied by the respondent nor there is any assertion in the affidavit-in-opposition that the said order was set aside by the higher authority and the property in question was thereafter again included in the list of abandoned property. The petitioner thereafter instituted Title suit No. 126 of 1 974 in the First court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca wherein the vendor and the Government were made parties as defendants No. 1 and 2 respectively. The plaint of the said suit has been annexed to the petition as Annexure 'B'. It further appears that the Government Pleader entered appearance in the said suit by filling power, the certified copy of which has been annexed to the petition as Annexure .`C'. The Government of Bangladesh (defendant No. 2) thereafter took several adjournments for filing written statement, and the certified copies of the said applications for adjournments have been annexed to the petition as Annexures (4) but ultimately defendant No. 2 did not file any written statement and accordingly the suit was decreed exparte on 4.9.74. The vendor ( defendant No. 1) having failed to comply with the direction of the court, the sale deed was executed and registered by the court on 14.1.75, the certified copy of which has been annexed to the petition as Annexure 'F'. 

 6. The documents filed by the petitioner clearly show that the petitioner acquired valid title and possession of the premises in question by virtue of the sale deed which was duly executed and registered through court. Mr. M. M. Haque has, however, argued that since the property had already vested in the Government as an abandoned property under P. O. No. 16 of 1972, the decree passed in the said suit was a nullity in the eye of law. We find no substance in the contention of Mr. Haque. We wonder how on the face of the order passed by the Sub-Divisional Officer on 26.2.73. (Annexure 7') Mr. Haque can advance the argument that the property vested in the Government as an abandoned properly and that the decree could be treated as a nullity. Nothing has been produced before us to show that the order of the Sub-Divisional Officer excluding the premises from the list of an abandoned property by his order dated 26.2.73 was set aside by any higher authority'. Moreover, the plea that it was an abadoned property was not taken before the learned Subordinate Judge where it appears that the respondents took several adjournments to file written statement and contest the suit but ultimately they did neither. After having allowed the suit to be decreed exparte, we do not see how the respondents can now come up with the plea that the property in question vested in the Government as early as 1972. Having regard to these facts and circumstances and the materials on record, we are unable to accept the respondent's contention that the premises in question is an abandoned property. 

 11. It was evident from a perusal of the different provisions of the Order and the Rules that the legislature was fully conscious of the sacred rights of the citizens and to protect them from the high-handed and arbitrary action of the executive, various provisions were incorporated in the Order. These provisions were intended to afford an opportunity to a person to present his case and be heard in defence of his case. It is new well-settled that whether in administrative or in judicial matters the principles of natural justice, if consistent with the provisions of the statute, must be duly adhered to and complied with. In all proceedings whether administrative or judicial the principles of natural justice have to be observed, if the proceedings result in consequence affecting the person or property or other rights of the parties concerned. The general consensus of judicial opinion in this sub-continent appears to be that in order to ensure the elementary principles of fairness the person sought to be affected must, at least know the nature of the allegations made against him and that he should be given a fair opportunity of putting his case before the authority concerned. The object of the rules of natural justice is to secure justice and to prevent the miscarriage of justice. When a statutory provision can be read consistently with the principles of natural justice the courts are bound to see that the same has been observed and complied with. In the instant case, Article 7 of the Order, in our opinion, enshrined the principles of natural justice and offered an opportunity to the person proceeded against to put his case before the authority concerned and he also had the right of being heard in person. This salutary provision of law was incorporated for the purpose of affording protection to the citizen against any arbitrary and highhanded action on the part of the executive. But, we are constrained to observe that in the instant case none of the provisions of law which were mandatory, was complied with in evicting the petitioner forcibly from the premises. Admittedly, the petitioner was not evicted by either the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate but by Mr. Aftabuddin the Deputy Secretary of the Government. Nothing has been asserted or produced before us to show that Mr. Aftabuddin was authorised to evict the petitioner as required under article 7 of the Order. It is singularly unfortunate that Mr. Aftabuddin, an officer of the rank of Deputy Secretary to the Government should have taken the law in his own hands and acted in such high-handed manner in utter disregard of the very law that he was supposed to be enforcing. He ignored the registered title-deed and even the decree of the court when those were produced before him by the petitioner. He did not comply with any of the mandatory provisions of law before evicting the petitioner from the premises in question. The allegations of arbitrary: action and high-handedness made on uncontroverted. Such action of the officers, if allowed to go unchecked, will bring slur on the good name of the Government. It shows how a law meant for the good of the country with safeguards for the protection of innocent citizens can become an instrument of oppression in the hands of irresponsible officers. Having regard to these facts and circumstances, we are constrained to hold that the impugned action of the respondents in evicting the petitioner from the premises in question was wholly unauthorised and illegal.
